questions.stem: A 19-year-old in a severe asthma attack was wheezing loudly on arrival in the emergency department. Twenty minutes and two albuterol treatments later, the nurse hears no wheezing and very faint breath sounds. The client is drowsy, and the SpO2 is 86%. How should the nurse interpret this change?

options.text: The bronchospasm is easing in response to the albuterol
Airflow is so limited that respiratory failure is near
The client is falling asleep from exhaustion after treatment
The pulse oximeter probe is giving a false low reading

rationale.correct: Absent wheezing in severe asthma is an ominous sign; call for help and prepare for intubation.

perOption.a: Improvement brings better air movement and oxygenation, not drowsiness and hypoxemia.
perOption.b: A silent chest means too little air moves to make wheezes; with drowsiness, it signals impending respiratory arrest.
perOption.c: Drowsiness with hypoxemia signals carbon dioxide retention, not rest.
perOption.d: The clinical picture matches the reading.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize a silent chest as impending respiratory failure.

questions.stem: A client with asthma arrives at urgent care with wheezing, chest tightness, a respiratory rate of 28/min and an SpO2 of 91%. The client's medications include fluticasone, salmeterol and montelukast. Which medication should the nurse give first?

options.text: Albuterol by nebulizer
An extra dose of the salmeterol inhaler
The evening montelukast dose early
Two extra puffs of fluticasone

rationale.correct: Short-acting beta2 agonists such as albuterol are the rescue medication for acute bronchospasm.

perOption.a: A short-acting beta2 agonist relaxes bronchial smooth muscle within minutes and is the rescue drug.
perOption.b: Salmeterol is a long-acting maintenance drug and too slow for rescue.
perOption.c: Leukotriene modifiers prevent symptoms; they do not relieve an attack.
perOption.d: Inhaled steroids reduce inflammation over days and do not relieve acute bronchospasm.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose the rescue medication for an asthma exacerbation.

questions.stem: A client with asthma whose personal best peak flow is 500 L/min calls the clinic. This morning's reading is 225 L/min, and the client is short of breath while talking. According to the asthma action plan, what should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: "Keep taking your usual medicines and check again tomorrow."
"Use your rescue inhaler and get emergency care right now."
"Double your inhaled steroid dose for the next 3 days."
"Rest today and hold the inhaler so you don't build up tolerance."

rationale.correct: Peak flow zones: green 80% to 100%, yellow 50% to 79% (rescue medication and follow the plan), red below 50% (emergency).

perOption.a: This is the green-zone response, for 80% or more of personal best.
perOption.b: 225 is 45% of personal best, the red zone, which needs immediate treatment and emergency care.
perOption.c: Doubling the steroid is not an emergency treatment.
perOption.d: Withholding rescue medication is dangerous.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a 24-year-old client newly diagnosed with persistent asthma who has a cat. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Learn your triggers, such as smoke, dust and pet dander, and limit exposure
Carry your rescue inhaler with you wherever you go
Use a spacer with your metered-dose inhaler
Rinse your mouth after using your inhaled steroid
Keep your controller inhaler daily, even when you feel well
Use your salmeterol inhaler when an asthma attack starts
Stop the controller medicine in summer when symptoms are mild

rationale.correct: Asthma self-management combines trigger control, correct inhaler technique and daily controllers, with a rescue inhaler always available.

perOption.a: Avoiding triggers reduces attacks.
perOption.b: Quick access to albuterol is essential during an attack.
perOption.c: A spacer improves delivery to the lungs.
perOption.d: Rinsing prevents oral thrush.
perOption.e: Controller drugs prevent attacks and are taken every day.
perOption.f: Salmeterol is a long-acting drug for maintenance, never for rescue.
perOption.g: Stopping controllers leads to loss of control.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old client has started montelukast 10 mg each evening for asthma. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take it in the evening at about the same time each day."
"I'll take an extra one when I start to wheeze."
"I'll tell my parents if I notice mood changes or bad dreams."
"I'll keep using my albuterol inhaler when I have an attack."

rationale.correct: Leukotriene modifiers are for long-term control, not rescue; report mood changes, sleep disturbance or suicidal thoughts.

perOption.a: Montelukast is taken once daily, usually in the evening.
perOption.b: Montelukast prevents symptoms; it does not relieve acute bronchospasm.
perOption.c: Montelukast can cause neuropsychiatric effects that should be reported.
perOption.d: Albuterol remains the rescue drug.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a COPD exacerbation and known carbon dioxide retention is receiving oxygen at 6 L/min by nasal cannula, which a family member turned up. The SpO2 is 98%, and the client has become increasingly drowsy and hard to rouse. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Increase the oxygen further, since the client looks tired
Titrate oxygen to SpO2 88% to 92% and get an ABG
Stop the oxygen completely until the client wakes up
Let the client sleep and reassess at the next vital signs

rationale.correct: Many clients with COPD have a target SpO2 of 88% to 92%; excess oxygen can increase CO2 retention and drowsiness.

perOption.a: More oxygen can worsen carbon dioxide retention.
perOption.b: Excess oxygen in some clients with COPD worsens hypercapnia; the target is lower, and an ABG measures the CO2.
perOption.c: Stopping oxygen risks severe hypoxemia.
perOption.d: Increasing drowsiness may mean hypercapnia and needs action now.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage oxygen therapy in a client with COPD.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client with COPD to use pursed-lip breathing during activity. What is the main purpose of this technique?

options.text: To strengthen the diaphragm muscle
To keep airways open longer as the client breathes out
To speed up the client's breathing rate
To loosen secretions so they can be coughed up

rationale.correct: Pursed-lip breathing lengthens exhalation and reduces air trapping.

perOption.a: Diaphragmatic breathing is a different technique.
perOption.b: Pursed lips create back-pressure that keeps small airways open, so trapped air can leave.
perOption.c: The goal is a slower, controlled rate.
perOption.d: Huff coughing and airway clearance devices loosen secretions.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Explain the purpose of pursed-lip breathing.

questions.stem: A client with severe COPD has lost 5 kg over 3 months and becomes short of breath while eating. Body mass index is 18.5. Which nutrition advice should the nurse give?

options.text: "Eat three large meals a day so that you don't have to eat as often."
"Eat small, frequent, high-calorie meals and rest before eating."
"Drink plenty of fluids with each meal to help food go down."
"Follow a low-calorie diet so you have less weight to carry."

rationale.correct: Breathing takes a lot of energy in COPD; small, frequent, nutrient-dense meals help prevent malnutrition.

perOption.a: Large meals push on the diaphragm and increase breathlessness.
perOption.b: Small meals reduce abdominal pressure, and extra calories meet the high energy cost of breathing.
perOption.c: Fluids with meals cause early fullness; they are better taken between meals.
perOption.d: Clients with COPD often need more calories, not fewer.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a 70-year-old client with long-standing COPD at a routine clinic visit. Which findings are expected for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Barrel-shaped chest
Use of neck muscles to help breathe
Prolonged expiration
Sudden sharp pain on one side of the chest
SpO2 of 99% on room air
New confusion since this morning

rationale.correct: Chronic COPD findings include a barrel chest, accessory muscle use, prolonged expiration and a lower baseline saturation; new or sudden changes are not expected.

perOption.a: Air trapping increases the chest's front-to-back diameter.
perOption.b: Accessory muscles help when the diaphragm is flattened.
perOption.c: Narrowed airways slow air leaving the lungs.
perOption.d: Sudden one-sided pain may mean a pneumothorax, a complication.
perOption.e: Clients with severe COPD often have lower baseline saturations.
perOption.f: Acute confusion may signal hypercapnia or infection and is not expected.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with COPD has been prescribed tiotropium by dry-powder inhaler. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll use it once a day, at the same time each day."
"I'll use it when I suddenly can't catch my breath."
"I'll be careful not to get the powder in my eyes."
"I might notice my mouth feels dry while taking it."

rationale.correct: Long-acting bronchodilators are maintenance drugs; short-acting beta2 agonists are for rescue.

perOption.a: Tiotropium is a once-daily maintenance drug.
perOption.b: Tiotropium is a long-acting anticholinergic for maintenance, not rescue.
perOption.c: Contact with the eyes can blur vision and raise eye pressure.
perOption.d: Dry mouth is a common anticholinergic effect.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client from a nursing home is admitted with suspected pneumonia. The temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), and the client has no cough or chest pain. Which finding is often the earliest or only sign of pneumonia in older adults?

options.text: A high fever with shaking chills
New confusion or a change in behavior
A cough with rust-colored sputum
Sharp chest pain on deep breathing

rationale.correct: Older adults often have atypical signs of infection, such as confusion, falls or poor appetite, without fever.

perOption.a: Older adults often have a blunted fever response.
perOption.b: Acute confusion or delirium is often the first sign of infection in older adults.
perOption.c: Classic signs may be absent in older adults.
perOption.d: Pleuritic pain may be absent or not reported.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize atypical presentations of pneumonia in older adults.

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia confined to the right lower lobe has an SpO2 of 89% on 4 L/min by nasal cannula. The client can turn independently, and the left lung is clear. Which position will best improve oxygenation?

options.text: Lying on the right side
Lying on the left side
Lying prone with the head turned
Lying flat on the back

rationale.correct: 'Good lung down' matches blood flow to ventilation in one-sided lung disease.

perOption.a: The affected lung would get more blood flow but cannot oxygenate it well.
perOption.b: With the good lung down, gravity sends more blood to the lung that ventilates best.
perOption.c: Prone positioning is used for ARDS, not one-sided pneumonia.
perOption.d: A flat position reduces lung expansion.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Position a client with one-sided pneumonia to improve oxygenation.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with community-acquired pneumonia has thick secretions, crackles in the right base and no fluid restrictions. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Incentive spirometer about 10 times an hour while awake
Fluid intake of 2 to 3 L a day
Walking in the hall as tolerated
Head of the bed raised
Coughing and deep breathing every 2 hours
Fluid restriction to dry up the secretions
Bed rest to save energy for recovery

rationale.correct: Pneumonia care: airway clearance, fluids, deep breathing, mobility and positioning.

perOption.a: Deep breathing opens collapsed alveoli and helps clear secretions.
perOption.b: Fluids thin secretions when there is no restriction.
perOption.c: Walking improves ventilation and moves secretions.
perOption.d: Elevation improves lung expansion.
perOption.g: Immobility worsens secretion clearance and increases complications.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan care for a client with pneumonia.

questions.stem: A client with dysphagia after a stroke has been cleared by the speech-language pathologist for a soft diet with nectar-thick liquids. Which action best reduces the risk of aspiration during meals?

options.text: Have the client recline at 30 degrees so the food goes down slowly
Have the client sit upright and tuck the chin when swallowing
Give a sip of thin water after each bite to clear the mouth
Offer all liquids through a straw so the client can control them

rationale.correct: Aspiration precautions: sit upright at 90 degrees, chin tuck, small bites, liquids thickened as ordered, and stay upright after meals.

perOption.a: A semi-reclined position raises aspiration risk.
perOption.b: Sitting upright with a chin tuck protects the airway.
perOption.c: Thin liquids are harder to control and more likely to be aspirated.
perOption.d: Straws can deliver liquid too quickly.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent aspiration in a client with dysphagia.

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia has an SpO2 of 85% on 6 L/min by nasal cannula, with a respiratory rate of 30/min. The provider asks the nurse to switch to a device that delivers a higher oxygen concentration right away. Which device should the nurse expect to use?

options.text: Nasal cannula at a higher flow rate
Nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Simple face mask at 5 L/min
Venturi mask set at 28%

rationale.correct: When hypoxemia persists on a nasal cannula, a nonrebreather or high-flow device gives a much higher FiO2.

perOption.a: A standard cannula is limited to about 6 L/min and 44% oxygen.
perOption.b: A nonrebreather delivers the highest concentration of the low-flow devices, about 60% to 90%.
perOption.c: A simple mask at this flow gives less oxygen than the current cannula.
perOption.d: A 28% Venturi gives less oxygen than the current setting.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose an oxygen device that delivers a high FiO2.

questions.stem: A client with acute hypoxemia is receiving oxygen by nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min. On rounds, the nurse checks the setup. Which observation requires the nurse's action?

options.text: The reservoir bag collapses fully each time the client breathes in
The one-way valves on the side of the mask are in place
The mask fits snugly over the nose and mouth with the strap on
The client's SpO2 has risen from 84% to 95% since it was applied

rationale.correct: A nonrebreather's reservoir bag must stay inflated; raise the flow or check the device if it collapses.

perOption.a: The bag should stay at least partly inflated; collapse means the client is not getting enough oxygen.
perOption.b: The valves stop the client rebreathing exhaled air.
perOption.c: A snug fit is correct.
perOption.d: This shows a good response.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A provider prescribes oxygen at 10 L/min by standard nasal cannula for a client with an SpO2 of 88%. The unit has no high-flow cannula equipment. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Set the cannula flow at 10 L/min as prescribed
Clarify the prescription with the provider
Put a nonrebreather mask on the client instead
Set it at 6 L/min and leave the order as written

rationale.correct: A standard nasal cannula delivers 1 to 6 L/min (about 24% to 44% oxygen); higher needs call for another device.

perOption.a: A standard nasal cannula is limited to about 6 L/min.
perOption.b: Flows above 6 L/min by standard cannula dry the mucosa without adding much oxygen; another device is needed.
perOption.c: The nurse cannot change the device without a prescription.
perOption.d: Changing the dose without telling the provider is not appropriate.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the limits of a standard nasal cannula.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the flowsheet of a 72-year-old client on day 2 of treatment for pneumonia. Highlight the findings that require follow-up.

rationale.correct: Watch for signs of deterioration in pneumonia: a rising respiratory rate, falling saturation and a change in mental status.

perOption.r1: A falling temperature shows a response to treatment.
perOption.r2: Tachypnea above about 24 to 28/min signals worsening respiratory status.
perOption.r4: This is expected with bacterial pneumonia.
perOption.r5: New confusion may mean worsening hypoxemia or sepsis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a large pleural effusion is about to have a thoracentesis at the bedside. How should the nurse position the client?

options.text: Sitting up, leaning over the bedside table
Lying flat on the back with arms at the sides
Trendelenburg with the head down
Lying prone on the bed

rationale.correct: For thoracentesis, the client sits upright, leaning forward; afterward, watch for pneumothorax and bleeding.

perOption.a: This widens the spaces between the ribs and lets fluid collect at the lung bases.
perOption.b: This does not give access to the back of the chest.
perOption.c: This is unsafe and does not help access.
perOption.d: This does not spread the ribs.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client returned from a bronchoscopy with biopsy 45 minutes ago and is asking for a drink of water. Which action should the nurse take before giving the client anything to drink?

options.text: Check that the gag reflex has returned
Check the client's blood glucose level
Give a small sip of ice water to test the swallow
Lower the head of the bed flat for 4 hours

rationale.correct: After bronchoscopy, keep the client NPO until the gag reflex returns, usually in about 2 hours.

perOption.a: The throat is numbed during the procedure; drinking before the gag reflex returns risks aspiration.
perOption.b: This is not specific to bronchoscopy.
perOption.c: Nothing is given by mouth until the gag reflex is confirmed.
perOption.d: A semi-Fowler's position is preferred.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client on month 2 of isoniazid and rifampin for latent tuberculosis calls the clinic with several concerns. Which report should the nurse address first?

options.text: "My urine and tears have turned orange-red."
"My skin looks yellow and my urine is dark."
"I feel a little queasy after taking the pills."
"Should I be taking vitamin B6 with these pills?"

rationale.correct: Isoniazid can cause hepatitis and peripheral neuropathy: avoid alcohol, monitor liver function and give vitamin B6.

perOption.a: Orange body fluids are expected with rifampin, not a toxicity.
perOption.b: Jaundice and dark urine signal hepatotoxicity, a serious adverse effect of isoniazid.
perOption.c: Mild nausea can be managed by taking the drug with a small snack.
perOption.d: Pyridoxine is often prescribed to prevent neuropathy; this is a teaching question.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with active pulmonary tuberculosis is starting a four-drug regimen with directly observed therapy. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take my medicines for at least 6 months."
"I'll stop the pills once my cough has gone away."
"I'll cover my mouth and nose when I cough or sneeze."
"I'll need sputum tests to show I'm no longer contagious."

rationale.correct: TB treatment needs months of adherence, often with directly observed therapy, to cure it and prevent resistance.

perOption.a: Treatment usually lasts 6 to 9 months.
perOption.b: Stopping early leads to relapse and drug resistance.
perOption.c: This reduces transmission.
perOption.d: Negative sputum tests guide when isolation ends.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client how to use an incentive spirometer on the first day after abdominal surgery. Place the steps in order, from first to last.

items.text: Hold the breath for 3 to 5 seconds, then breathe out slowly
Seal the lips around the mouthpiece
Breathe in slowly and deeply, raising the indicator

rationale.correct: Incentive spirometry: sit up, exhale, seal, inhale slowly and deeply, hold, then exhale; repeat about 10 times an hour while awake.

perOption.a: Sitting upright allows full lung expansion.
perOption.b: This empties the lungs before the deep breath.
perOption.c: A tight seal measures the breath accurately.
perOption.d: Slow, deep breaths open collapsed alveoli.
perOption.e: Holding the breath keeps the alveoli open longer.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old client has had fever, body aches and a cough for 24 hours and tests positive for influenza A. The provider prescribes oseltamivir. What should the nurse tell the client about this medication?

options.text: "It works best when started within 48 hours of the first symptoms."
"It means you can skip your yearly flu vaccine from now on, too."
"It kills the bacteria that cause the flu and its complications."
"You'll take a single dose today and that will be the course."

rationale.correct: Start influenza antivirals within 48 hours of symptom onset; yearly vaccination is still recommended.

perOption.a: Antivirals shorten the illness most when started early.
perOption.b: Oseltamivir does not replace vaccination.
perOption.c: Influenza is caused by a virus.
perOption.d: Treatment is usually twice a day for 5 days.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
